transcript:
Meeting header:
Date: 2026-12-17 15:00 UTC
Duration: ~46 minutes
Attendees: Maya (Redwood AE), Diego (Redwood SE), Priya (Redwood CSM), Raj (Nimbus Head ML), Ling (Nimbus Platform), Tom (Nimbus Backend)

Auto-summary (auto-generated): Reviewing throughput baseline and tuning applied last week. Main knob changes: continuous batching throttle lowered, concurrency cap raised from 200 to 260, KV cache TTL extended and hit rate observed at ~63%. Agree to run full-day ramp test with shaped queue and burst fallback to smaller, cheaper model when latency spikes.

Transcript:
[00:00] Maya: hey everyone thanks for joining, um we've got 45 minutes on the calendar. quick round table? who we got from nimbus?
[00:06] Raj: hey, raj here. quick hello.
[00:08] Ling: ling here, tom's joining in a bit.
[00:11] Tom: (muffled) yeah sorry delayed start.
[00:14] Maya: cool. diego will lead the tuning recap, i'll jump in on the commercial / next steps. diego over to you.
[00:22] Diego: ok thanks. so last run we implemented continuous batching with dynamic batch threshold - basically we lowered the max wait to 18ms and increased the batch multiplier so we get more consolidations at lower concurrency. we also bumped concurrency cap from 200 to 260 for the pilot pool. quick numbers: baseline last week avg tokens/sec was 12.1k, after changes avg went to 15.8k, p95 latency moved from 290ms to 340ms during spikes, p50 improved slightly.
[00:54] Raj: wait p95 increased? is that because of larger batches causing tail?
[00:58] Diego: yeah partially, we observed tail amplification when large batches coincided with KV cache misses; the cache hit rate sits at about 63% which means on a miss we go to cold model path and that adds ~180-220ms per request. we've been tuning TTL and prefetch heuristics.
[01:20] Ling: are those hit rates from our sample traffic or from redwood simulated workload?
[01:23] Diego: real sample you sent, the 48 hours you provided. small note the parser misattributed some user ids so we filtered out bot traffic which shifted the hit rate a few percent.
[01:35] Tom: what's the cost impact of raising concurrency to 260? our controller team is nervous about spend.
[01:40] Maya: good question. raising concurrency means fewer total instances but higher per-instance token throughput so unit cost per token usually drops. however if p95 jumps and you need more SLAs, you might spin up more fallback capacity. we'll send a delta estimate after the 24h ramp.
[01:55] Raj: ok. can we explore changing the queue shape instead of just concurrency?
[02:00] Diego: yes that's the plan — the adaptive queue shape we talked about earlier will shift token allocation: small requests get priority in the front of the queue and we cap how many long-context requests can accumulate concurrently. this prevents head-of-line blocking which was happening when a couple of long sessions flooded the pool.
[02:18] Ling: can you explain head-of-line blocking again? we saw some spikes where small calls wait 200-300ms.
[02:24] Diego: sure. imagine a long 3k token generation that enters the queue and because of batching it pulls small single-token requests into the same batch — then the long job dominates batch latency. adaptive queueing limits joining of long sessions so small requests form smaller batches and get served faster.
[02:40] Tom: what's the implementation risk? do we need config changes on our side?
[02:44] Diego: no infra changes on your side. it's a runtime policy change. we will push a new queue profile and it can be rolled back in 1 minute if needed.
[02:51] Raj: cool. what about fallbacks for burst? last week we saw a 3x burst where some requests timed out.
[02:57] Diego: we've got a tiered fallback: when queue depth exceeds threshold we send 30% of overflow to a lower-cost quantized model variant with reduced quality; those are stateless so they don't use KV cache and are faster for short replies. also we can route by customer segment so critical callers always stay on high-quality path.
[03:14] Ling: does the lower-cost variant respect PII encryption and audit logging? security is non-negotiable for us.
[03:19] Maya: yes, it travels through the same control plane. we can enable KMS for keys and all audit logs flow to your tenant log bucket. we'll share SOC2 docs but the lower-quality model runs in the same VPC pool for the pilot so no egress differences.
[03:34] Raj: good. any unexpected regressions from last week's change?
[03:37] Diego: minor: we saw a gating bug where prefetch requests occasionally duplicated in a batch, adding slight CPU overhead; fixed yesterday and won't impact today's run.
[03:46] Tom: can you walk through the planned 24h ramp shape? what are the percentile targets?
[03:50] Diego: sure. plan: start with steady-state at 300 rps for first 4 hours, then step to 900 rps over 2 hours, spike to 2.5k rps for 30 minutes, drop to 600 rps and repeat pattern. we're tracking p50/p95/p99 latency and token throughput and KV hit rate. target is p95 < 500ms for customer-critical routes, and p99 < 900ms.
[04:15] Ling: those p95 targets still a bit high for us, our product team wants sub-400ms p95.
[04:19] Priya: quick note — sometimes p95 varies by route; we should isolate the 3 top-volume routes and give separate SLOs.
[04:25] Maya: agreed. action: nimbus to send top-3 routes. ling will own.
[04:28] Ling: yep can do.
[04:30] Raj: single-thread question — how does batching interact with KV cache TTL prefetch? are we prefetching embeddings or attention keys?
[04:38] Diego: good question. we prefetch KV for likely next tokens when sessions exceed a heuristic — the prefetch window is 2 tokens ahead by default; prefetch reduces miss penalty but increases CPU. we'll tune prefetch aggressiveness per-route.
[04:51] Tom: last week you mentioned warm pools to reduce coldstart on burst. status?
[04:55] Diego: warm pools are enabled — we keep a small reserve of pre-baked model replicas warmed with commonly used prompts. that reduced cold model startup by ~120ms in our last tests.
[05:06] Raj: nice. what telemetry will we get from the 24h run?
[05:09] Diego: we'll deliver a CSV with minute-level metrics: rps, queue depth, batch sizes distribution, p50/p95/p99, KV hit rate, instance count, fallback ratio. plus a short notes doc with anomalies.
[05:21] Ling: can we also get per-route breakdown?
[05:23] Diego: yep per-route is possible if you send route IDs.
[05:27] Ling: will do.
[05:29] Maya: on the business side, if the pilot requires raising reserved concurrency beyond current commit we can map that to a short-term dedicated commit; i'll share pricing delta. but first let's see results.
[05:39] Raj: what's the expected improvement in cost per 1M tokens if we get p95 within target?
[05:43] Maya: ballpark — with higher utilization and fewer instances spinning idle, you could see 12-18% cost reduction. if we move to a dedicated reserved pool it can be 25-30% depending on commit. will provide numbers after the ramp.
[05:57] Tom: any risks of increased inference errors due to quantization on fallback?
[06:01] Diego: yes quality drops are expected — shorter answers sometimes have missing details. we'll keep a small eval set and run quality regression checks; if we see >3% drop on rouge-like metric we can throttle fallback.
[06:14] Raj: remind me how we measure quality for this pilot?
[06:16] Priya: we use a blended metric of semantic similarity + token-level accuracy on 200 eval prompts you provided. we'll run that daily during the ramp.
[06:26] Ling: sounds good. timeline then: you run the 24h ramp starting Monday 12/21?
[06:31] Diego: we can start Monday morning UTC; need route IDs and final traffic sample by Sunday EOD.
[06:37] Ling: we'll get it to you by Sunday.
[06:39] Raj: ok. who owns the run and postmortem?
[06:41] Diego: redwood SE owns the run and the results doc, nimbus will own validating SLOs and providing feedback.
[06:48] Maya: that will be in the action items.
[06:50] Tom: quick question about monitoring — will alerts be fired if fallback ratio above 20%?
[06:55] Diego: we can set alert threshold to whatever you prefer. default pilot alert is 15% fallback for 5 minutes. we can set to 10% if you want.
[07:04] Ling: set to 10% for critical routes.
[07:06] Diego: noted.
[07:08] Raj: any follow-up on procurement or compliance needed?
[07:11] Maya: we shared SOC2 and DPA last quarter; if you need extra logs retention or specific KMS integrations we can scope that, may impact pricing.
[07:22] Ling: we'll check with security team, likely fine for pilot.
[07:25] Priya: i'll add a note to CSM tracker.
[07:28] Maya: ok, quick recap and next steps. diego will run 24h ramp starting 2026-12-21 UTC morning, will push adaptive queueing profile and fallback policy. diego to share minute-level CSV and anomaly notes by 2026-12-22. ling to send top-3 route IDs and 7-day sample by 2026-12-19. maya to share pricing delta for reserved capacity by 2026-12-21.
[07:50] Raj: sounds good. thanks everyone.
[07:52] Maya: thanks all. meeting end.
